claim: The H2A.Z histone variant is a genome-wide hallmark of permissive chromatin.
source: The H2A.Z histone variant, a genome-wide hallmark of permissive chromatin, is enriched near transcription start sites in all eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of H2A.Z, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: H2A.Z is enriched near transcription start sites in all eukaryotes.
source: The H2A.Z histone variant, a genome-wide hallmark of permissive chromatin, is enriched near transcription start sites in all eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and represents established knowledge about H2A.Z distribution.

claim: H2A.Z is deposited by the SWR1 chromatin remodeler.
source: H2A.Z is deposited by the SWR1 chromatin remodeler and evicted by unclear mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and represents established knowledge about H2A.Z deposition.

claim: H2A.Z eviction is dependent on RNA Polymerase II (Pol II).
source: We tracked H2A.Z in living yeast at single-molecule resolution, and found that H2A.Z eviction is dependent on RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) and the Kin28/Cdk7 kinase, which phosphorylates Serine 5 of heptapeptide repeats on the carboxy-terminal domain of the largest Pol II subunit Rpb1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-molecule tracking experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: H2A.Z eviction is dependent on the Kin28/Cdk7 kinase.
source: We tracked H2A.Z in living yeast at single-molecule resolution, and found that H2A.Z eviction is dependent on RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) and the Kin28/Cdk7 kinase, which phosphorylates Serine 5 of heptapeptide repeats on the carboxy-terminal domain of the largest Pol II subunit Rpb1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-molecule tracking experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Kin28/Cdk7 kinase phosphorylates Serine 5 of heptapeptide repeats on the carboxy-terminal domain of the largest Pol II subunit Rpb1.
source: We tracked H2A.Z in living yeast at single-molecule resolution, and found that H2A.Z eviction is dependent on RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) and the Kin28/Cdk7 kinase, which phosphorylates Serine 5 of heptapeptide repeats on the carboxy-terminal domain of the largest Pol II subunit Rpb1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Kin28/Cdk7 kinase.

claim: H2A.Z eviction is linked to transcription initiation, promoter escape and early elongation activities of Pol II.
source: These findings link H2A.Z eviction to transcription initiation, promoter escape and early elongation activities of Pol II.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about Pol II and Kin28 dependence.

claim: Global transcription at yeast promoters is responsible for eviction of H2A.Z.
source: Because passage of Pol II through +1 nucleosomes genome-wide would obligate H2A.Z turnover, we propose that global transcription at yeast promoters is responsible for eviction of H2A.Z.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and logical inference.

claim: H2A.Z is enriched at most promoters and enhancers genome-wide.
source: H2A.Z is enriched at most promoters and enhancers genome-wide, and plays a role in establishing a permissive chromatin state for regulated transcription (Weber and Henikoff, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weber and Henikoff, 2014.

claim: H2A.Z plays a role in establishing a permissive chromatin state for regulated transcription.
source: H2A.Z is enriched at most promoters and enhancers genome-wide, and plays a role in establishing a permissive chromatin state for regulated transcription (Weber and Henikoff, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weber and Henikoff, 2014.

claim: H2A.Z is incorporated in nucleosomes flanking DNase hypersensitive, nucleosome-depleted regions (NDRs).
source: H2A.Z is incorporated in nucleosomes flanking DNase hypersensitive, nucleosome-depleted regions (NDRs), especially at the so-called '+1 nucleosome' overlapping with or immediately downstream of the transcription start site (TSS) (Albert et al., 2007; Weber and Henikoff, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albert et al., 2007 and Weber and Henikoff, 2014.

claim: H2A.Z is especially enriched at the '+1 nucleosome' overlapping with or immediately downstream of the transcription start site (TSS).
source: H2A.Z is incorporated in nucleosomes flanking DNase hypersensitive, nucleosome-depleted regions (NDRs), especially at the so-called '+1 nucleosome' overlapping with or immediately downstream of the transcription start site (TSS) (Albert et al., 2007; Weber and Henikoff, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albert et al., 2007 and Weber and Henikoff, 2014.

claim: The deposition of H2A.Z in budding yeast is catalyzed by the conserved SWR1 chromatin remodeling complex.
source: The deposition of H2A.Z in budding yeast is catalyzed by the conserved SWR1 chromatin remodeling complex in an ATP-dependent reaction involving exchange of nucleosomal H2A-H2B for H2A.Z-H2B dimers (Mizuguchi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mizuguchi et al., 2004.

claim: SWR1-catalyzed H2A.Z deposition is an ATP-dependent reaction involving exchange of nucleosomal H2A-H2B for H2A.Z-H2B dimers.
source: The deposition of H2A.Z in budding yeast is catalyzed by the conserved SWR1 chromatin remodeling complex in an ATP-dependent reaction involving exchange of nucleosomal H2A-H2B for H2A.Z-H2B dimers (Mizuguchi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mizuguchi et al., 2004.

claim: The +1 nucleosome undergoes higher turnover compared to nucleosomes in the gene body.
source: Genome-wide studies have shown that compared to nucleosomes in the gene body, the +1 nucleosome undergoes higher turnover, which is not correlated with the level of mRNA transcription by Pol II (Dion et al., 2007; Grimaldi et al., 2014; Rufiange et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dion et al., 2007; Grimaldi et al., 2014; Rufiange et al., 2007.

claim: +1 nucleosome turnover is not correlated with the level of mRNA transcription by Pol II.
source: Genome-wide studies have shown that compared to nucleosomes in the gene body, the +1 nucleosome undergoes higher turnover, which is not correlated with the level of mRNA transcription by Pol II (Dion et al., 2007; Grimaldi et al., 2014; Rufiange et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dion et al., 2007; Grimaldi et al., 2014; Rufiange et al., 2007.

claim: The disruptive passage of Pol II through +1 nucleosomes during infrequent mRNA transcription is unlikely to account for H2A.Z eviction on a global scale.
source: Thus, the disruptive passage of Pol II through +1 nucleosomes during infrequent mRNA transcription is unlikely to account for H2A.Z eviction on a global scale.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that +1 nucleosome turnover is not correlated with mRNA transcription levels.

claim: Biochemical studies have suggested that yeast H2A.Z eviction could be due to chromatin remodeling in reverse mediated by SWR1 itself.
source: Biochemical studies have suggested that yeast H2A.Z eviction could be due to chromatin remodeling in reverse mediated by SWR1 itself (Watanabe et al., 2013) or the related INO80 remodeler (Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011), but other biochemical studies found no supporting evidence (Luk et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watanabe et al., 2013.

claim: Biochemical studies have suggested that yeast H2A.Z eviction could be due to chromatin remodeling in reverse mediated by the INO80 remodeler.
source: Biochemical studies have suggested that yeast H2A.Z eviction could be due to chromatin remodeling in reverse mediated by SWR1 itself (Watanabe et al., 2013) or the related INO80 remodeler (Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011), but other biochemical studies found no supporting evidence (Luk et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011.

claim: Other biochemical studies found no supporting evidence for SWR1 or INO80-mediated H2A.Z eviction.
source: Biochemical studies have suggested that yeast H2A.Z eviction could be due to chromatin remodeling in reverse mediated by SWR1 itself (Watanabe et al., 2013) or the related INO80 remodeler (Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011), but other biochemical studies found no supporting evidence (Luk et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luk et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Genome-wide assembly of the transcription pre-initiation complex (PIC) has been proposed to evict H2A.Z.
source: Alternatively, genome-wide assembly of the transcription pre-initiation complex (PIC) has been proposed to evict H2A.Z, but the key event in this multistep process remains elusive (Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tramantano et al., 2016.

claim: The key event in PIC-mediated H2A.Z eviction remains elusive.
source: Alternatively, genome-wide assembly of the transcription pre-initiation complex (PIC) has been proposed to evict H2A.Z, but the key event in this multistep process remains elusive (Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tramantano et al., 2016.

claim: Single-particle tracking (SPT) of fluorescently tagged proteins in live cells has emerged as a robust imaging technique to determine kinetic behaviors of protein factors.
source: Single-particle tracking (SPT) of fluorescently tagged proteins in live cells has emerged as a robust imaging technique to determine kinetic behaviors of protein factors (Elf and Barkefors, 2019; Liu and Tjian, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elf and Barkefors, 2019 and Liu and Tjian, 2018.

claim: SPT is complementary to genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation-DNA sequencing technologies (ChIP-seq) without the general caveats of chemical fixation and chromatin manipulations.
source: For chromatin-interacting proteins, SPT is complementary to genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation-DNA sequencing technologies (ChIP-seq) without the general caveats of chemical fixation and chromatin manipulations.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of SPT methodology.

claim: SPT directly measures the fast-diffusing, chromatin-free population as well as the quasi-immobile, chromatin-bound fraction tracking with macroscopic chromosome movements.
source: SPT directly measures the fast-diffusing, chromatin-free population as well as the quasi-immobile, chromatin-bound fraction tracking with macroscopic chromosome movements (Liu and Tjian, 2018; Taddei and Gasser, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu and Tjian, 2018 and Taddei and Gasser, 2012.

claim: H2A.Z shows 82% chromatin-bound fraction and 18% chromatin-free fraction based on Spot-On analysis.
source: The SPT profiles for H2A.Z and H2B were best fitted by a simple model comprised of two diffusive populations—a major, slow-diffusing chromatin-bound fraction (H2A.Z: 82%, H2B: 76%, average D: 0.03 μm2s−1), and a minor, fast-diffusing chromatin-free fraction (H2A.Z: 1.18 μm2s−1, H2B: 1.29 μm2s−1) (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-particle tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: H2B shows 76% chromatin-bound fraction based on Spot-On analysis.
source: The SPT profiles for H2A.Z and H2B were best fitted by a simple model comprised of two diffusive populations—a major, slow-diffusing chromatin-bound fraction (H2A.Z: 82%, H2B: 76%, average D: 0.03 μm2s−1), and a minor, fast-diffusing chromatin-free fraction (H2A.Z: 1.18 μm2s−1, H2B: 1.29 μm2s−1) (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-particle tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The average diffusion coefficient of chromatin-bound H2A.Z and H2B is 0.03 μm2s−1.
source: The SPT profiles for H2A.Z and H2B were best fitted by a simple model comprised of two diffusive populations—a major, slow-diffusing chromatin-bound fraction (H2A.Z: 82%, H2B: 76%, average D: 0.03 μm2s−1), and a minor, fast-diffusing chromatin-free fraction (H2A.Z: 1.18 μm2s−1, H2B: 1.29 μm2s−1) (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-particle tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of chromatin-free H2A.Z is 1.18 μm2s−1.
source: The SPT profiles for H2A.Z and H2B were best fitted by a simple model comprised of two diffusive populations—a major, slow-diffusing chromatin-bound fraction (H2A.Z: 82%, H2B: 76%, average D: 0.03 μm2s−1), and a minor, fast-diffusing chromatin-free fraction (H2A.Z: 1.18 μm2s−1, H2B: 1.29 μm2s−1) (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-particle tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of chromatin-free H2B is 1.29 μm2s−1.
source: The SPT profiles for H2A.Z and H2B were best fitted by a simple model comprised of two diffusive populations—a major, slow-diffusing chromatin-bound fraction (H2A.Z: 82%, H2B: 76%, average D: 0.03 μm2s−1), and a minor, fast-diffusing chromatin-free fraction (H2A.Z: 1.18 μm2s−1, H2B: 1.29 μm2s−1) (Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-particle tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The fraction of chromatin-bound H2A.Z was consistent with a previous estimate by in vivo cross-linking.
source: The fraction of chromatin-bound H2A.Z was consistent with a previous estimate by in vivo cross-linking (Mohan et al., 2018), and the D value of bound yeast H2B was also consistent with that of mammalian H2B (0.02 μm2s−1) in a previous report (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mohan et al., 2018.

claim: The D value of bound yeast H2B (0.03 μm2s−1) is consistent with that of mammalian H2B (0.02 μm2s−1).
source: The fraction of chromatin-bound H2A.Z was consistent with a previous estimate by in vivo cross-linking (Mohan et al., 2018), and the D value of bound yeast H2B was also consistent with that of mammalian H2B (0.02 μm2s−1) in a previous report (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2018.

claim: The 'free' H2A.Z fraction represents soluble H2A.Z-H2B dimers biochemically associated with histone chaperones, in addition to a minor population in complex with the ~1 MDa SWR1 complex.
source: The 'free' H2A.Z fraction represents soluble H2A.Z-H2B dimers biochemically associated with histone chaperones, in addition to a minor population in complex with the ~1 MDa SWR1 complex (Luk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citation to Luk et al., 2007.

claim: Similar frequencies of chromatin-bound and free H2A.Z were observed in cells growing synchronously after release from G1 arrest into S phase.
source: We observed similar frequencies of chromatin-bound and free H2A.Z in cells growing synchronously after release from G1 arrest into S phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell cycle synchronization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The SWR1 complex (Swr1-Halo subunit) showed more chromatin-free diffusion compared to histones.
source: In contrast to behaviors of the histones, the SWR1 complex (Swr1-Halo subunit) showed more chromatin-free diffusion.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-particle tracking experiments.

claim: Deletion of Swc2 substantially reduced the chromatin-bound fraction of SWR1 from 47% to 21%.
source: In addition, deletion of Swc2, a key subunit involved in the recruitment of SWR1 to gene promoters (Ranjan et al., 2013), substantially reduced the chromatin-bound fraction from 47% to 21% (Figure 1C,D,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the single-particle tracking experiments shown in Figure 1C,D,F, with citation to Ranjan et al., 2013 for Swc2 function.

claim: Swc2 is a key subunit involved in the recruitment of SWR1 to gene promoters.
source: In addition, deletion of Swc2, a key subunit involved in the recruitment of SWR1 to gene promoters (Ranjan et al., 2013), substantially reduced the chromatin-bound fraction from 47% to 21% (Figure 1C,D,F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ranjan et al., 2013.

claim: The remaining 21% of slow molecules for the swc2∆ mutant may be largely attributed to transient binding.
source: (Our imaging regime captures both stable and transiently bound SWR1 in the slow-diffusing population; the remaining 21% of slow molecules for the swc2∆ mutant may be largely attributed to transient binding).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Swc5 is not required for Swr1 recruitment but is essential for SWR1 activity.
source: To highlight H2A.Z eviction in live cells, we blocked the H2A.Z incorporation pathway at gene promoters by conditional 'anchor-away' (AA) depletion of the Swc5 subunit, which is not required for Swr1 recruitment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but essential for SWR1 activity (Haruki et al., 2008; Sun and Luk, 2017; Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haruki et al., 2008; Sun and Luk, 2017; Tramantano et al., 2016, and data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon Swc5 AA, chromatin-bound H2A.Z decreased from 79% to 49%.
source: Upon Swc5 AA, we found the expected decrease of chromatin-bound H2A.Z from 79% to 49% (Figure 2A–C and rapamycin time course in Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with ChIP-seq results showing genome-wide reduction of H2A.Z at +1 nucleosomes under similar conditions (Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The decrease in chromatin-bound H2A.Z upon Swc5 AA is consistent with ChIP-seq results showing genome-wide reduction of H2A.Z at +1 nucleosomes.
source: Upon Swc5 AA, we found the expected decrease of chromatin-bound H2A.Z from 79% to 49% (Figure 2A–C and rapamycin time course in Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with ChIP-seq results showing genome-wide reduction of H2A.Z at +1 nucleosomes under similar conditions (Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tramantano et al., 2016.

claim: The remaining chromatin-bound H2A.Z after Swc5 AA may be due to residual H2A.Z at the +1 nucleosome or to histone chaperone-mediated H2A.Z deposition in nucleosomes over the entire genome.
source: The remaining chromatin-bound H2A.Z may be due to residual H2A.Z at the +1 nucleosome or to histone chaperone-mediated H2A.Z deposition in nucleosomes over the entire genome, as suggested by in vivo cross-linking studies (Mohan et al., 2018; Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to Mohan et al., 2018 and Tramantano et al., 2016.

claim: When Swc5 and Rpb1 are co-depleted by double AA, the chromatin-bound H2A.Z fraction increased (66%) relative to Swc5 AA alone (49%).
source: When Swc5 and Rpb1 are co-depleted by double AA, the chromatin-bound H2A.Z fraction increased (66%) relative to Swc5 AA alone (49%) (compare Figure 3A to Figure 2C and Figure 3A to Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the double anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 3A compared to Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Pol II plays a major role in H2A.Z eviction.
source: These results indicate that Pol II indeed plays a major role in H2A.Z eviction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the double anchor-away experiments.

claim: Single AA of Rpb1 in rapamycin-treated cells showed a marginal increase from 84% to 87% of the bulk chromatin-bound H2A.Z over the untreated control.
source: (Single AA of Rpb1 in rapamycin-treated cells showed a marginal increase from 84% to 87% of the bulk chromatin-bound H2A.Z over the untreated control [Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C]).
evidence: This is a finding from the single anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Co-depletion of Swc5 and Ino80 showed no rise in bound H2A.Z compared to the single AA of Swc5.
source: To examine the role of the INO80 remodeler in H2A.Z eviction, we analyzed the H2A.Z distribution for Swc5 and Ino80 co-depletion by double AA and found no rise in bound H2A.Z compared to the single AA of Swc5 (compare Figure 3A to Figure 2C and Figure 3C to Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the double anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 3A compared to Figure 2C and Figure 3C compared to Figure 2D.

claim: Single AA of Ino80 showed no change in chromatin-bound H2A.Z.
source: (We observed no change in chromatin-bound H2A.Z for single AA of Ino80 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F)).
evidence: This is a finding from the single anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: Pol II, but not the INO80 remodeler, has a major role in H2A.Z eviction.
source: Taken together, we conclude that Pol II, but not the INO80 remodeler, has a major role in H2A.Z eviction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the double anchor-away experiments.

claim: Contributions by other factors such as the ANP32E histone chaperone found in mammalian cells are not excluded.
source: Contributions by other factors such as the ANP32E histone chaperone found in mammalian cells are not excluded (Mao et al., 2014; Obri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging other potential mechanisms, supported by citations to Mao et al., 2014 and Obri et al., 2014.

claim: Ser5-P is catalyzed by the yeast Kin28/Cdk7 kinase, a component of the kinase module (Kin28-Ccl1-Tfb3) of TFIIH.
source: Ser5-P is catalyzed by the yeast Kin28/Cdk7 kinase, a component of the kinase module (Kin28-Ccl1-Tfb3) of TFIIH, and is linked to capping of nascent RNA, Pol II release from the Mediator complex, promoter escape and early elongation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Kin28/Cdk7 kinase.

claim: Ser5-P is linked to capping of nascent RNA, Pol II release from the Mediator complex, promoter escape and early elongation.
source: Ser5-P is catalyzed by the yeast Kin28/Cdk7 kinase, a component of the kinase module (Kin28-Ccl1-Tfb3) of TFIIH, and is linked to capping of nascent RNA, Pol II release from the Mediator complex, promoter escape and early elongation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Ser5-P.

claim: The Bur1/Cdk9 kinase phosphorylates the Rpb1 linker just upstream of CTD, at residues Thr 1471 and Ser 1493.
source: Recently, the Bur1/Cdk9 kinase was shown to phosphorylate the Rpb1 linker just upstream of CTD, at residues Thr 1471 and Ser 1493 (Chun et al., 2019), facilitating Pol II transition from early elongation to productive elongation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chun et al., 2019.

claim: Bur1/Cdk9 kinase phosphorylation facilitates Pol II transition from early elongation to productive elongation.
source: Recently, the Bur1/Cdk9 kinase was shown to phosphorylate the Rpb1 linker just upstream of CTD, at residues Thr 1471 and Ser 1493 (Chun et al., 2019), facilitating Pol II transition from early elongation to productive elongation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chun et al., 2019.

claim: The Ctk1/Cdk12 kinase mediates Ser2 phosphorylation of the CTD associated with productive elongation through protein-coding regions.
source: Furthermore, the Ctk1/Cdk12 kinase mediates Ser2 phosphorylation of the CTD associated with productive elongation through protein-coding regions (Corden, 2013; Harlen and Churchman, 2017; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Corden, 2013; Harlen and Churchman, 2017; Wong et al., 2014.

claim: Only Kin28 is required for H2A.Z eviction, as indicated by 65% chromatin-bound H2A.Z in the Kin28 and Swc5 double AA relative to 49% in the single AA of Swc5.
source: Only Kin28 is required for H2A.Z eviction, as indicated by 65% chromatin-bound H2A.Z in the Kin28 and Swc5 double AA relative to 49% in the single AA of Swc5 (compare Figure 4B to Figure 2C and Figure 4F to Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the double anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 4B compared to Figure 2C and Figure 4F compared to Figure 2D.

claim: Depletion of Kin28 alone showed an increase in chromatin-bound H2A.Z from 78% to 82%.
source: Consistent with its role in H2A.Z eviction, depletion of Kin28 alone showed an increase in chromatin-bound H2A.Z, though marginal (from 78% to 82%, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the single anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Double AA of Swc5 and the Bur1 kinase did not inhibit loss of chromatin-bound H2A.Z.
source: In contrast, double AA of Swc5 and the Bur1 kinase did not inhibit loss of chromatin-bound H2A.Z, nor did double AA of Swc5 and the Ctk1 kinase (Figure 4C, D and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the double anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 4C, D and F.

claim: Double AA of Swc5 and the Ctk1 kinase did not inhibit loss of chromatin-bound H2A.Z.
source: In contrast, double AA of Swc5 and the Bur1 kinase did not inhibit loss of chromatin-bound H2A.Z, nor did double AA of Swc5 and the Ctk1 kinase (Figure 4C, D and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the double anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 4C, D and F.

claim: Nascent RNA is co-transcriptionally capped by the sequential activity of three enzymes—Cet1, Ceg1 and Abd1—and is completed when RNA reaches ~100 nt.
source: In the wake of Pol II initiation, nascent RNA is co-transcriptionally capped by the sequential activity of three enzymes—Cet1, Ceg1 and Abd1—and is completed when RNA reaches ~100 nt (Lidschreiber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lidschreiber et al., 2013.

claim: The Cet1-Ceg1 complex recognizes the 5' triphosphate on the RNA and Ser5-P on the Pol II CTD.
source: Capping of the 5' end of nascent RNA is initiated by the Cet1-Ceg1 complex, which recognizes the 5' triphosphate on the RNA and Ser5-P on the Pol II CTD (Martinez-Rucobo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martinez-Rucobo et al., 2015.

claim: Double AA of Swc5 and Cet1 showed no increase in chromatin-bound H2A.Z compared to single AA of Swc5.
source: To examine whether RNA capping or associated activities are required for H2A.Z eviction, we performed double AA of Swc5 and Cet1, and found no increase in chromatin-bound H2A.Z compared to single AA of Swc5 (compare Figure 4E to Figure 2C and Figure 4F to Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the double anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 4E compared to Figure 2C and Figure 4F compared to Figure 2D.

claim: H2A.Z eviction is not dependent on RNA capping.
source: Thus, H2A.Z eviction is not dependent on RNA capping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the double anchor-away experiments with Cet1.

claim: Double AA of Swc5 and Rrp6 showed no increase of chromatin-bound H2A.Z.
source: Likewise, we found no increase of chromatin-bound H2A.Z upon double AA of Swc5 and Rrp6, the 3'−5' exonuclease responsible for degradation of noncoding RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the double anchor-away experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Rrp6 is the 3'−5' exonuclease responsible for degradation of noncoding RNA.
source: Likewise, we found no increase of chromatin-bound H2A.Z upon double AA of Swc5 and Rrp6, the 3'−5' exonuclease responsible for degradation of noncoding RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Rrp6.

claim: An early stage of transcription elongation closely linked to Pol II CTD Ser5 phosphorylation by Kin28 is required for robust eviction of chromatin-bound H2A.Z.
source: Taken together, we conclude that an early stage of transcription elongation closely linked to Pol II CTD Ser5 phosphorylation by Kin28 is required for robust eviction of chromatin-bound H2A.Z.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the double anchor-away experiments with various kinases and RNA processing factors.

claim: Transcription of most yeast genes is infrequent and nucleosome turnover along gene bodies is low.
source: Transcription of most yeast genes is infrequent and nucleosome turnover along gene bodies is low, but the +1 nucleosome constitutively turns over at a 3-fold higher rate (Dion et al., 2007; Grimaldi et al., 2014; Yen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dion et al., 2007; Grimaldi et al., 2014; Yen et al., 2013.

claim: The +1 nucleosome constitutively turns over at a 3-fold higher rate than nucleosomes in gene bodies.
source: Transcription of most yeast genes is infrequent and nucleosome turnover along gene bodies is low, but the +1 nucleosome constitutively turns over at a 3-fold higher rate (Dion et al., 2007; Grimaldi et al., 2014; Yen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dion et al., 2007; Grimaldi et al., 2014; Yen et al., 2013.

claim: H2A.Z is constitutively displaced from +1 nucleosomes for both active and rarely transcribed genes, on a timescale of <15 min.
source: Similarly, H2A.Z is constitutively displaced from +1 nucleosomes for both active and rarely transcribed genes, on a timescale of <15 min (Tramantano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tramantano et al., 2016.

claim: The live-cell SPT approach shows that Pol II rather than the INO80 sub-family of remodelers plays a key role in H2A.Z eviction.
source: The live-cell SPT approach shows that Pol II rather than the INO80 sub-family of remodelers plays a key role in H2A.Z eviction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The INO80 sub-family of remodelers comprise of SWR1 and INO80 remodeling complexes, with similarities in the catalytic split-ATPase domain and four shared subunits (Rvb1, Rvb2, Act1 and Arp4).
source: The INO80 sub-family of remodelers comprise of SWR1 and INO80 remodeling complexes, with similarities in the catalytic split-ATPase domain and four shared subunits (Rvb1, Rvb2, Act1 and Arp4).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the INO80 sub-family of remodelers.

claim: INO80 has been previously suggested to mediate the reversal of SWR1-catalyzed H2A.Z deposition.
source: INO80 has been previously suggested to mediate the reversal of SWR1-catalyzed H2A.Z deposition (Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011.

claim: Several publications report that INO80 displays no detectable H2A.Z eviction from chromatin in either yeast or mammalian cells.
source: However, in addition to this study, there are several publications reporting that INO80 displays no detectable H2A.Z eviction from chromatin in either yeast or mammalian cells (Au-Yeung and Horvath, 2018; Tramantano et al., 2016; Jeronimo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Au-Yeung and Horvath, 2018; Tramantano et al., 2016; Jeronimo et al., 2015.

claim: The INO80 complex is known to mediate nucleosome repositioning in vitro and in vivo.
source: Although evidently uninvolved in H2A.Z eviction, the INO80 complex is known to mediate nucleosome repositioning in vitro and in vivo (Kubik et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kubik et al., 2019 and Shen et al., 2003.

claim: The Pol II PIC plays an important role in H2A.Z eviction.
source: Our results confirm the previous finding that the Pol II PIC plays an important role in H2A.Z eviction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, confirming previous work.

claim: PIC assembly per se is not sufficient for H2A.Z eviction but Kin28-dependent phosphorylation of Ser5 of the CTD heptapeptide repeats is important.
source: Furthermore, the observed dependence on Kin28/Cdk7 kinase for robust H2A.Z displacement suggests that PIC assembly per se, that is the recruitment of general transcription factors and Pol II to promoter, is not sufficient for H2A.Z eviction but Kin28-dependent phosphorylation of Ser5 of the CTD heptapeptide repeats is important (Figure 5, box).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Depletion of Kin28 by AA does not alter TSS usage.
source: A role for Kin28 in Ssl2-facilitated TSS scanning by Pol II is not excluded for H2A.Z eviction, although it has been shown that depletion of Kin28 by AA does not alter TSS usage (Murakami et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Murakami et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibition of H2A.Z eviction upon depletion of Kin28/Cdk7 kinase, but not Bur1/Cdk9 or Ctk1/Cdk12 kinases narrows the relevant state of Pol II to early elongation after promoter escape, but not to productive elongation.
source: Inhibition of H2A.Z eviction upon depletion of Kin28/Cdk7 kinase, but not Bur1/Cdk9 or Ctk1/Cdk12 kinases narrows the relevant state of Pol II to early elongation after promoter escape, but not to productive elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings with different kinases.

claim: The PIC remains largely intact upon Kin28/Cdk7 depletion, as shown by accumulation of TFIID, Mediator and Pol II at gene promoters.
source: (We note that the PIC remains largely intact upon Kin28/Cdk7 depletion, as shown by accumulation of TFIID, Mediator and Pol II at gene promoters [Knoll et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knoll et al., 2019 and Wong et al., 2014.

claim: H2A.Z eviction is independent of RNA modifying and metabolizing activities just downstream of CTD Ser5 phosphorylation.
source: Thus, H2A.Z eviction is independent of RNA modifying and metabolizing activities just downstream of CTD Ser5 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings with Cet1 and Rrp6.

claim: Transcriptional elongation by Pol II is known to cause displacement of nucleosomal histones in biochemical assays.
source: Transcriptional elongation by Pol II is known to cause displacement of nucleosomal histones in biochemical assays (Lorch et al., 1987), providing a mechanism for H2A.Z turnover at the +1 nucleosome in the process of transcription through protein-coding regions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lorch et al., 1987.

claim: Genes that do not engage in productive transcription of mRNA exhibit genome-wide, constitutive transcription of noncoding RNAs which are prematurely terminated by the Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 pathway in budding yeast.
source: We propose a similar mechanism for genes that do not engage in productive transcription of mRNA, but exhibit genome-wide, constitutive transcription of noncoding RNAs which are prematurely terminated by the Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 pathway in budding yeast (Schaughency et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citation to Schaughency et al., 2014.

claim: The early elongation activity of Pol II would dislodge H2A.Z-H2B dimers from the histone octamer of the +1 nucleosome.
source: The early elongation activity of Pol II would dislodge H2A.Z-H2B dimers from the histone octamer of the +1 nucleosome.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Displacement of the more stably bound H3-H4 tetramer likely requires assistance from histone chaperones and/or other remodelers.
source: Displacement of the more stably bound H3-H4 tetramer likely requires assistance from histone chaperones and/or other remodelers (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: After displacement of core histones, reassembly of a canonical nucleosome on gapped chromatin should occur, mediated by the mass action of the predominating H2A-H2B histone pool and histone chaperones.
source: After displacement of core histones, reassembly of a canonical nucleosome on gapped chromatin should occur, mediated by the mass action of the predominating H2A-H2B histone pool and histone chaperones, nucleosome positions being reset by chromatin remodelers such as ISWI, RSC, and INO80 (Lai and Pugh, 2017﻿ Figure 5).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citation to Lai and Pugh, 2017 and reference to Figure 5.

claim: Nucleosome positions are reset by chromatin remodelers such as ISWI, RSC, and INO80.
source: After displacement of core histones, reassembly of a canonical nucleosome on gapped chromatin should occur, mediated by the mass action of the predominating H2A-H2B histone pool and histone chaperones, nucleosome positions being reset by chromatin remodelers such as ISWI, RSC, and INO80 (Lai and Pugh, 2017﻿ Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lai and Pugh, 2017.

claim: Maintenance of a NDR of sufficient length (>60 bp DNA) by remodelers and subsequent histone acetylation recruits SWR1 to canonical +1 nucleosomes.
source: Maintenance of a NDR of sufficient length (>60 bp DNA) by remodelers and subsequent histone acetylation recruits SWR1 to canonical +1 nucleosomes, the essential substrate for SWR1 (Ranjan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citation to Ranjan et al., 2013.

claim: Canonical +1 nucleosomes are the essential substrate for SWR1.
source: Maintenance of a NDR of sufficient length (>60 bp DNA) by remodelers and subsequent histone acetylation recruits SWR1 to canonical +1 nucleosomes, the essential substrate for SWR1 (Ranjan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ranjan et al., 2013.

claim: Stimulation of the catalytic Swr1 ATPase by nucleosome and H2A.Z-H2B dimer substrates triggers histone dimer exchange.
source: Stimulation of the catalytic Swr1 ATPase by nucleosome and H2A.Z-H2B dimer substrates then triggers histone dimer exchange (Luk et al., 2010; Ranjan et al., 2013), completing the cycle of H2A.Z/H2A replacement (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luk et al., 2010 and Ranjan et al., 2013, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: H2A.Z eviction is coupled to transcription not only from protein-coding genes transcribed by Pol II but also ribosomal, 5S and tRNA genes transcribed by Pol I and Pol III.
source: We envision that H2A.Z eviction is coupled to transcription not only from protein-coding genes transcribed by Pol II but also ribosomal, 5S and tRNA genes transcribed by Pol I and Pol III.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the mechanism.

claim: The constitutive global transcription of noncoding RNA by Pol II is additionally coupled to H2A.Z eviction.
source: Because H2A.Z eviction is not correlated with mRNA transcription by Pol II (Tramantano et al., 2016), the constitutive global transcription of noncoding RNA by Pol II is additionally coupled to H2A.Z eviction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and citation to Tramantano et al., 2016.

claim: There is substantial evidence for low-level, heterogenous transcripts of several hundred nucleotides, initiating from multiple start-sites within yeast NDRs.
source: There is substantial evidence for low-level, heterogenous transcripts of several hundred nucleotides, initiating from multiple start-sites within yeast NDRs (Pelechano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pelechano et al., 2013.

claim: For budding yeast, noncoding RNA transcripts evidently result from Pol II initiation without substantial pausing.
source: For budding yeast, these noncoding RNA transcripts evidently result from Pol II initiation without substantial pausing (Booth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Booth et al., 2016.

claim: At metazoan promoters, turnover of H2A.Z enriched in +1 nucleosomes may be similarly coupled to transcription in the process of Pol II pausing and release.
source: At metazoan promoters, turnover of H2A.Z enriched in +1 nucleosomes may be similarly coupled to transcription in the process of Pol II pausing and release (Tome et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Tome et al., 2018.

claim: At metazoan enhancers, infrequent Pol II transcription of eRNAs could be responsible for eviction of H2A.Z.
source: Likewise at metazoan enhancers, infrequent Pol II transcription of eRNAs (Tippens et al., 2018) could be responsible for eviction of H2A.Z, representing erasure of a permissive histone variant mark on the epigenome.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Tippens et al., 2018.
